Kids who someday gather our remains
Will have no idea that we were once
As swift as foxes racing across the hillside;
And that during fall, when ripening grapes
Sharpened the already crisp air with their scent,
We too existed, drawing in the frosty breath;
Even less will they imagine that along with our bones
We left behind far more—we left behind the very
Appearance of the world, and the emotions we felt
In response to what we witnessed. The clouds of spring drift
Over the boarded-up manor,
And past our entrance and the gusty heavens
A cultured kind of hopelessness rings out.
For ages we understood how that manor appeared,
And whatever we uttered about it became
Woven into what it truly is... The children,
Still fashioning their budding halos,
Will speak the words we spoke yet remain unaware,
And they'll remark that the manor looks
As though whoever dwelled there left behind
A restless spirit raging within empty walls—
A grimy home in a ravaged, hollowed-out world,
A fragment of shadows rising into white,
Brushed with the gold of the lavish, glowing sun.

# Legacy of the Living

Future children who unearth our bones will never truly understand that we were once vibrant and fully alive—as swift as foxes racing across the hill. To them, we will be nothing more than remnants, fragments of a life they cannot imagine. They will hold the evidence of our existence in their hands, yet remain unable to grasp the vitality that once animated these very bones.

These children will fail to realize that we left behind far more than our physical remains. Beyond the mere matter of our bodies, we bequeathed our perceptions, our emotional responses to the world we witnessed and felt so deeply. Our inner lives—the way we saw, understood, and reacted to everything around us—cannot be excavated from the earth or reconstructed from what remains.

Consider the mansion-house: our sustained observations of it shaped its very identity. What we said about it, how we described and remembered it, became woven into what it actually is. Through our attention and language, we did not merely observe the place—we participated in creating its essence. The mansion exists, in part, as a product of the meaning we poured into it.

Though future generations will inherit and speak our language, they will remain ignorant of the meanings and experiences we embedded within it. The words will survive, passed from mouth to mouth, but the living significance we invested in them will not. They will possess the vessel while losing its contents, speaking our tongue without ever knowing what we truly meant.

And so these children will perceive the mansion as a desolate, haunted ruin. They will describe it as a spirit storming in blank walls, standing alone within a gutted and decaying world. Where we once found life, warmth, and meaning, they will see only emptiness and haunting—a hollow shell stripped of everything that made it ours.
outputs.L4:
# The Silence of Our Bones

When those who come long after us unearth the fragments we leave behind—the scattered bones, the worn foundations of our homes, the tools that once fit so naturally in our hands—they will hold in their palms the mere physical residue of existence. Yet these objects will tell them nothing of what it meant to be alive in our time. They will not feel the warmth of an afternoon that once made us pause, nor sense the particular ache of a longing we carried, nor understand the way a familiar face could fill an ordinary moment with meaning. The vibrant interior worlds we inhabited—rich with perception, saturated with emotion, alive with the significance we cast upon everything we touched—will have vanished utterly, leaving only silent matter behind.

This is the poem's quiet devastation: that so much of what makes a life a life cannot survive the body that lived it. We spend our days projecting meaning onto the world, seeing beauty where others might see nothing, feeling grief that reshapes our understanding of an entire landscape, loving in ways that transform the mundane into the sacred. But these subjective interpretations—the very texture of consciousness—leave no fossil, no artifact, no trace that future hands can recover.

And here lies the poem's deeper and more haunting insight. Our descendants will not merely inherit our physical remains; they will inherit far more intimate things. They will speak the words we shaped, walk the streets we walked, and dwell within the spaces we built and named. In doing so, they will unknowingly carry forward our very ways of seeing—the assumptions embedded in our language, the meanings we stitched into our places, the interpretations of reality that we mistook for reality itself. They will perpetuate our subjective vision of the world without ever recognizing it as ours, without knowing that they see through eyes we shaped, that they think in patterns we established.

Yet even as they inherit these frameworks, they will be forever barred from the living consciousness that first created them. They will use our words but never feel what we felt when we spoke them. They will inhabit our meanings but never touch the awareness that gave those meanings life. The structure endures; the animating spirit is lost.

In this way, the poem holds two truths in delicate tension. There is a strange endurance to human experience—something of us persists, transmitted invisibly across generations through language and place and inherited perception. But there is also an absolute and irrecoverable loss, for the one thing that truly mattered—the felt reality of being conscious, of being *here*, alive and awake in a world made vivid by our own attention—dies with each of us completely. What remains behind is real but hollow; what disappears is precisely what made it matter. Across the long reach of time, we both survive and vanish, our echoes carried forward by those who can never hear the voice that first gave them sound.
outputs.L5:
# Children, Will, and the Shaping of Character

Few forces in human life are as remarkable as the will of a child. From the earliest years, children demonstrate a fierce determination to explore, to test boundaries, and to assert themselves in a world they are only beginning to understand. This will is not something to be broken, but rather guided and nurtured into a source of strength.

## Understanding a Child's Will

The will of a child is closely tied to their emerging sense of identity. When a toddler insists on tying their own shoes or a young child refuses to follow instructions, they are not simply being difficult. They are discovering that they are separate individuals capable of making choices. This growing independence, though sometimes exhausting for parents and teachers, is a healthy and necessary part of development.

A strong will can be both a challenge and a gift. Children who show determination early in life often carry that same persistence into adulthood, where it can fuel achievement, resilience, and leadership.

## The Role of Guidance

The relationship between children and their will requires thoughtful adults who understand the balance between freedom and structure. Too much control can crush a child's confidence and make them fearful of expressing themselves. On the other hand, too little guidance can leave children without the boundaries they need to feel secure.

The goal, then, is to channel a child's will constructively. This means:

- **Offering choices** within reasonable limits, so children feel a sense of control
- **Explaining reasons** behind rules rather than simply demanding obedience
- **Praising effort and persistence** to reinforce positive determination
- **Modeling patience** and self-discipline through our own behavior

## Growing Together

Ultimately, the journey of raising children involves patience, empathy, and understanding. When we respect a child's will and help them learn to direct it wisely, we give them one of the greatest gifts of all: the ability to shape their own lives with confidence and purpose. And in that shared journey of growth, both children and the adults who care for them are transformed for the better.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a modernist poem about children finding the bones of past generations and inheriting their language and world.
counterfactuals.output:
**Inheritance**

I.

The children come down to the dry riverbed
where the century has been laid out
like laundry, bleaching.

A femur. A jaw still articulate.
They do not know these are the words for it—
*femur, jaw*—
they only know the shape fits the hand
the way a spoon does.

II.

                    Small archaeologists,
they turn the syllables over:
                    *mother, water, war.*
The vowels have gone soft in the ground.
The consonants keep.

Somebody once said *bread*
and meant the whole warm loaf of being alive.
Now it is a sound picked up
between two fingers,
                    held to the light.

III.

Whose was this rib. Whose was this
grammar of hunger, this
declension of the field.
The grass does not answer,
the grass only continues,
translating everyone
into the same green.

IV.

They carry it home in their pockets—
the dead man's *yes*, the dead woman's
particular way of saying *evening*—
and the words wake up,
warm as coins from the fist,
and begin, without permission,
to mean.

V.

So the world is handed over
the only way it can be:
                    unfinished, mispronounced,
                    a house with the roof torn off
                    and the rain coming in
                    where the children stand
                    naming it,
                                        naming it.

counterfactuals.output:
# The Tenant of the Ruined House

I

What remains is not the house but the idea
Of a house, its cold geometry of loss,
The way a wall proposes what it was
Before the weather took it for its own.

The mind arrives here as a kind of guest
Among the absences, and finds them furnished:
A chair of shadow, and a shadow's table,
The nothing that the something used to be.

II

Consider how the dead compose the living.
They leave us rooms we have to reinvent,
A syntax of decay we learn to read
As one might learn a language from its ruins,

Its verbs half-swallowed by the creeping green,
Its nouns dispersed like plaster into air.
We are the readers of what they could not say.
We are the meaning of their broken glass.

III

The apple tree that no one planted, planted
By someone once, still offers up its white
Indifferent flowering to the vacant sills,
As if the season kept a promise made

To hands that are no longer there to keep it.
This is how mortality persists: it flowers.
It does not mourn. It merely goes on being
The bright particular of what is gone.

IV

And you who walk here in a later light,
You are the future of this ruined thing.
You make it mean by looking. You are the weather
That finds the house and finishes the house.

For nothing perishes that is well perceived,
And nothing lasts except in being changed.
The tenant of the ruined house is time,
And time is only what the mind can hold—

A candle carried through a roofless dark,
Illuminating what it cannot save.
